name: Early pregnancy signs and contacting a midwife
summary: The NHS says a missed period is the earliest sign of pregnancy, and a GP or midwife can be contacted once a test is positive.
keyPoints: The NHS says a missed period is the earliest and most reliable sign of pregnancy for someone with a regular monthly cycle.
Most home pregnancy tests can be used from the first day of a missed period, according to the NHS.
After finding out about a pregnancy, the NHS says to contact a GP or midwife, who help arrange the first appointment.
Many NHS trusts let people refer themselves for maternity care without seeing a GP first, though the process varies by area.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for heavy bleeding that soaks a pad, severe tummy pain or shoulder pain with feeling faint.
For lighter bleeding or milder pain, the NHS points to the maternity unit, a GP or NHS 111 the same day.

body.heading: What are the early signs of pregnancy?
body.body: The NHS says the earliest and most reliable sign of pregnancy is a missed period, for someone with a regular monthly cycle. NHS inform notes that an irregular cycle can make a missed period harder to notice. The NHS lists other signs, including feeling or being sick, unusual tiredness, tender breasts and needing to pass urine more often. Constipation, a metallic taste in the mouth and a stronger sense of smell are also on the list. Some people have very light spotting or bleeding around the time a period is due. The NHS says sickness can start as early as week 4 and can happen at any time of day. Symptoms vary a lot between people, and some people notice no obvious signs at all.

body.heading: How soon can a test confirm it?
body.body: The NHS says most home pregnancy tests can be used from the first day of a missed period. Someone who does not know when the next period is due can test at least 21 days after unprotected sex. Some early tests work sooner, so the packaging or a pharmacist can say how soon a particular test can be used. Tests come in different formats, and the instructions in the box explain how each one works. An out-of-date test may give an inaccurate result, so the expiry date is worth checking. The contraceptive pill and HRT do not affect a pregnancy test, though fertility medicines can contain the hormone hCG and may change the result. A positive result is very likely to be correct when the instructions were followed, while a negative result is less reliable. After a negative result, the NHS suggests waiting a few days and testing again. It says a GP can be contacted if a second test is negative but the period has not arrived. Some GP practices and sexual health clinics also offer pregnancy tests.

body.heading: Who should someone contact after a positive test?
body.body: The NHS says that once someone knows they are pregnant, they can get in touch with a GP or a midwife. Either one can help arrange the first appointment, which is the booking appointment with a midwife. The NHS says this appointment should happen before about 10 weeks of pregnancy, partly because some tests need to be done by then. For anyone past 10 weeks who has not yet seen a midwife, the NHS says to contact a GP or midwife as soon as possible. The first appointment may be at home, in a hospital, at a GP surgery or at a children's centre, depending on the local service. The NHS says screening tests are always optional, and it is a person's own choice whether to have them.

body.heading: How does someone book with a midwife?
body.body: Many NHS trusts let people refer themselves for pregnancy care without seeing a GP first. Some trusts use an online form, and others use a phone number, so the process differs from area to area. One trust says its form gives the team time to arrange a first appointment for between 8 and 10 weeks of pregnancy. Another explains that after an online form, an appointment for an ultrasound scan comes first, with a separate call or letter to arrange the first meeting with a midwife. That call may appear as coming from an unknown number. Someone registered with a GP is usually told about the pregnancy by the midwife team after the first appointment. A person without a GP can register with a local practice.

body.heading: Which symptoms need urgent help?
body.body: The NHS separates problems that need an ambulance from those that need advice the same day. It says to call 999 or go to A&E for heavy bleeding that soaks a pad soon after it is put on. Severe tummy pain, shoulder pain, or feeling sick, faint or dizzy in pregnancy are also signs of needing immediate treatment. Sudden, intense tummy pain with feeling very dizzy, fainting or looking very pale can mean an ectopic pregnancy has ruptured, which the NHS treats as very serious. For a possible pregnancy with a combination of a missed period, tummy pain low down on one side, vaginal bleeding or brown watery discharge, shoulder tip pain, or discomfort when peeing or pooing, the NHS says to contact a GP or call NHS 111. The NHS says tummy pain that is severe, or does not ease after resting for 30 to 60 minutes, needs urgent attention.

body.heading: What about bleeding, miscarriage and early pregnancy units?
body.body: The NHS says the ectopic pregnancy page describes symptoms that usually start around weeks 4 to 12, and that an ectopic pregnancy does not always cause symptoms. Bleeding is the main sign of miscarriage, but other conditions can also cause it, so the NHS advises getting it checked. For bleeding, the NHS advises contacting a GP or maternity team, or calling NHS 111, as soon as possible. For bleeding with mild or no pain, the NHS says to call the maternity unit if there is a number. Early pregnancy units, usually based in hospitals, can help with problems such as spotting, light bleeding or mild tummy pain. Whether someone can use one depends on the stage of pregnancy and where they live. Several trusts accept self-referral only in particular cases, such as a previous ectopic pregnancy or repeated miscarriages, and others take referrals only from a professional. The NHS says a person who is unsure can call NHS 111 or the maternity unit.
